entries.name: Philistia
entries.text: The coastal plain of southern Canaan held by the [[Philistines]] from about 1175 BCE, centered on the five cities of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath. Philistia was Israel's chief rival in the days of the judges and the early kings. Assyria later made its cities vassals. Rome eventually applied the name Palaestina, drawn from Philistia, to the whole province after the Bar Kokhba revolt, and the word Palestine descends from it.

entries.name: Moab
entries.text: Kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon and Zered rivers in present-day Jordan, with its capital at Dibon. The Mesha Stele, set up about 840 BCE, records King Mesha's revolt against Israel and is among the oldest inscriptions to name the God of Israel. Moab is also the setting for much of the Book of Ruth, whose heroine was a Moabite woman who joined the Jewish people.

entries.name: Edom
entries.text: Kingdom in the highlands south of the Dead Sea, in present-day southern Jordan and the Negev, linked in the Bible with Esau. Its copper mines at Timna and Faynan fed regional trade. Edom fought Judah repeatedly and fell to Babylon. Its people, later called Idumeans, were brought into the Jewish people under John Hyrcanus in the second century BCE, and [[Herod the Great]] came from an Idumean family.

entries.name: Ammon
entries.text: Kingdom east of the Jordan River with its capital at Rabbath Ammon, today's Amman, the capital of Jordan. The Ammonites fought Israel under Saul and David, and David's general Joab captured their capital. The modern name Amman preserves the ancient one.

entries.name: Aram-Damascus
entries.text: Aramean kingdom centered on Damascus, the main rival of the northern kingdom of Israel from the ninth to the eighth century BCE. Kings such as Hazael pressed Israel hard until Assyria destroyed Damascus in 732 BCE. The Tel Dan inscription, an Aramean victory stele of about 840 BCE, carries the earliest known mention of the House of David outside the Bible.

entries.name: Phoenicia
entries.text: Coastal city-states of Tyre, Sidon and Byblos on today's Lebanese coast, home to master seafarers and traders who founded colonies across the Mediterranean, including Carthage. The [[Phoenician alphabet]] became the ancestor of the Hebrew, Greek and Latin scripts. King Hiram of Tyre supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's Temple in [[Jerusalem]]. Their neighbors in the land were the [[Canaanites]], whose culture they largely continued.

entries.name: Nabataeans
entries.text: Arab trading people whose kingdom, centered on Petra in present-day Jordan, grew rich from the incense and spice caravans that crossed the [[Negev]] to the Mediterranean. They built walled desert cities at [[Avdat]], Mamshit, Shivta and Haluza, and used cisterns and terraced fields to farm the desert. Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE. Their Negev cities are a UNESCO World Heritage site.

entries.name: Samaritans
entries.text: Small community that keeps its own version of the Torah and holds [[Mount Gerizim]], not Jerusalem, to be the place chosen for worship. They still offer the Passover sacrifice there each year. Jewish and Samaritan tradition give different accounts of their origin. Their number fell to a few hundred in the early 20th century and has since grown to somewhat fewer than one thousand, living at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim and in Holon.

entries.name: Essenes
entries.text: Jewish sect of the Second Temple period that, according to [[Josephus]] and other ancient writers, lived in strict communities, shared property and stressed ritual purity. Many scholars link them to the settlement at [[Qumran]] and the [[Dead Sea Scrolls]], though others dispute the connection. They vanish from the record after the revolt against Rome.

entries.name: Pharisees
entries.text: Jewish movement of the Second Temple period that stressed study and the oral law alongside the written Torah. Their teachers shaped the [[Mishnah]]. After the destruction of the [[Second Temple]] in 70 CE their approach became the basis of rabbinic Judaism. [[Josephus]] and the New Testament describe them as a leading party with wide popular support.

entries.name: Sadducees
entries.text: Priestly and aristocratic party of the Second Temple period that accepted only the written Torah and rejected the oral law. They were tied to the Temple and its priesthood, and the party faded after the Temple was destroyed in 70 CE.

entries.name: Zealots
entries.text: Name given to Jewish rebel factions in the revolt against Rome of 66 to 73 CE, known as the [[First (66-73 CE) Revolt=First Revolt]]. Groups inside Jerusalem fought each other as well as the [[Romans]]. The Sicarii, a separate group, held [[Masada]] until its fall. The main source on all of them is [[Josephus]], who opposed the rebellion.

entries.name: Sanhedrin
entries.text: Council of Jewish sages and judges that served as the highest court and legislature of Jewish life. It sat in [[Jerusalem]] in the Second Temple period. After 70 CE it was re-formed at [[Yavne]], later moved to the Galilee, and ended about 425 CE.

entries.name: Diaspora
entries.text: Jewish communities living outside the land of Israel. It began with the exile to [[Babylon]] in 586 BCE and grew after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem. For some two thousand years Jews lived in Babylonia, Egypt, Europe, North Africa and the Americas, while a Jewish presence continued in the land. Today roughly as many Jews live outside Israel as in it.

entries.name: Abbasids
entries.text: Dynasty of caliphs that overthrew the [[Umayyads]] in 750 and ruled from Baghdad. The land was a frontier province, and by the 10th century Egyptian dynasties controlled it, until the [[Fatimids]] conquered it in 969.

entries.name: Twelve Tribes of Israel
entries.text: The tribes descended from the sons of [[Jacob]] according to the Bible, each with its own territory in the land. Joseph's descendants form two tribes, Ephraim and Manasseh. The ten northern tribes were carried off by Assyria after the [[Fall of Samaria]] in 722 BCE, while Judah and Benjamin formed the kingdom of Judah. The priestly tribe of Levi received towns but no territory.

entries.name: Yishuv
entries.text: Hebrew word for settlement, used for the organized Jewish community in the land before the state of 1948. The old Yishuv of religious families in [[Jerusalem]], [[Safed]], [[Tiberias]] and [[Hebron]] predated Zionism, and the new Yishuv grew from the [[First Aliyah]] of 1882. By 1948 it had more than 600,000 people, with its own schools, defense force and labor federation.

entries.name: Decapolis
entries.text: League of ten Greek-speaking cities of the Roman era, mostly east of the Jordan River in present-day Jordan and Syria. [[Beit She'an]], then called Scythopolis, was the only one west of the river. The cities shared Greek culture and had a measure of self-rule under Rome.

entries.name: Declaration of Independence
entries.text: The proclamation of the State of Israel, read by [[David Ben-Gurion]] on 14 May 1948 in the Tel Aviv Museum on [[Rothschild Boulevard]], hours before the [[British Mandate]] ended. It announced "the establishment of a Jewish state in Eretz Israel, to be known as the State of Israel," promised equal rights to all citizens and appealed to its Arab neighbors for peace. The United States recognized the new state within minutes. The next day the armies of five Arab states invaded, widening the [[War of Independence]].

entries.name: Jerusalem, Siege of (1948)
entries.text: From early 1948 Arab forces cut the only road from the coast to Jerusalem at Bab al-Wad, leaving about 100,000 Jews short of food, water and ammunition. Convoys fought their way up the road, and the burned armored trucks left along it are still kept as memorials. In May the Jordanian Arab Legion shelled the city and the Jewish Quarter of the [[Old City of Jerusalem]] surrendered on 28 May. The siege was broken in June when the [[Burma Road]] was opened around [[Latrun]].

entries.name: Altalena Affair
entries.text: In June 1948, during the first truce of the [[War of Independence]], the ship Altalena arrived with about 940 volunteers and a large cargo of arms for the [[Irgun]]. The new government under [[David Ben-Gurion]] insisted that all weapons belong to the [[Israel Defense Forces]]. After fighting at Kfar Vitkin, the ship was shelled off the Tel Aviv beach on 22 June and burned. Sixteen Irgun men and three soldiers were killed. [[Menachem Begin]] told his followers not to answer with civil war, and the state kept one army.

entries.name: Jewish communities lost in 1948
entries.text: During the [[War of Independence]] a number of Jewish communities fell or had to be abandoned. The four kibbutzim of the Etzion Bloc south of Jerusalem fell on 13 to 14 May 1948, and many defenders of Kfar Etzion were massacred after surrendering. Atarot and Neve Yaakov north of Jerusalem, and Kalya and Beit HaArava by the [[Dead Sea]], were evacuated. The Jewish Quarter of the [[Old City of Jerusalem]] surrendered, and Kfar Darom in [[Gaza]] was evacuated. Several were rebuilt after the [[Six-Day War]].

entries.name: Divided Jerusalem
entries.text: From 1948 to 1967 Jerusalem was split between Israel and Jordan. The line was drawn in November 1948 by [[Moshe Dayan]] and the Jordanian commander Abdullah el-Tell and confirmed in the 1949 armistice. Strips of no man's land ran through the city, the Mandelbaum Gate was the only crossing, and [[Mount Scopus]] with the [[Hebrew University]] campus became a cut-off Israeli enclave. Jordan held [[East Jerusalem]] and the Old City. Jews were barred from the [[Western Wall]], and synagogues of the Jewish Quarter, among them the [[Hurva Synagogue]], were destroyed.

entries.name: Waiting period (1967)
entries.text: The three tense weeks before the [[Six-Day War]]. In mid-May 1967 Egypt moved large forces into [[Sinai]] and had the UN Emergency Force withdrawn. On 22 May it closed the [[Straits of Tiran]] to Israeli shipping, which Israel had long called a cause for war. Jordan signed a defense pact with Egypt on 30 May and Iraqi troops followed. Israel mobilized its reserves while diplomacy failed. On 1 June [[Levi Eshkol]] formed a unity government with [[Moshe Dayan]] as defense minister, and four days later the war began.

entries.name: Jerusalem, Battle for (1967)
entries.text: On 5 June 1967 Jordan opened fire on West Jerusalem despite Israeli messages urging it to stay out of the war. Israeli paratroopers took Ammunition Hill in one of the hardest fights of the [[Six-Day War]], and on 7 June they entered the Old City through the Lions' Gate. Their commander Motta Gur radioed "The Temple Mount is in our hands." Within weeks Israel extended its law to [[East Jerusalem]] and widened the city's boundaries, and Jews returned to pray at the [[Western Wall]].

entries.name: Temple Mount status quo
entries.text: The arrangement set by [[Moshe Dayan]] days after the [[Six-Day War]]. Israel keeps security control of the [[Temple Mount]], while the Islamic Waqf, linked to Jordan, runs its daily affairs. Jews and other non-Muslims may visit at set hours but not pray there, and the [[Western Wall]] became the main place of Jewish prayer. A 1967 law protects access to holy places for all faiths. The status quo is contested: some Jews campaign for the right to pray on the Mount, and many Palestinians fear any change.

entries.name: Western Wall Plaza
entries.text: The open square in front of the [[Western Wall]]. Before 1967 worshipers stood in a narrow alley about 3.5 meters wide beside the Mughrabi Quarter. Days after the [[Six-Day War]] Israel cleared the quarter and created the plaza, which can hold tens of thousands of people. It hosts daily prayer, bar mitzvahs, national ceremonies and the swearing-in of soldiers, and it leads to the [[Western Wall Tunnels]].

entries.name: UN Resolution 242
entries.text: UN Security Council resolution of 22 November 1967, after the [[Six-Day War]]. It called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces "from territories occupied in the recent conflict" and for the right of every state in the region to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries. The English text deliberately left out the word "the" before territories. This formula of land for peace became the basis of the [[Camp David Accords]], the [[Oslo Accords]] and the peace treaty with [[Jordan]].

entries.name: Hebron after 1967
entries.text: Jews lived in [[Hebron]] for centuries until the 1929 massacre, in which 67 were killed, and the last families left in 1936. After the [[Six-Day War]] Rabbi Moshe Levinger and a group of families celebrated Passover 1968 in the city and stayed. The government built Kiryat Arba beside it in 1971, and Jewish homes returned to the city center from 1979. Since the 1997 Hebron Protocol the city has been divided between Palestinian and Israeli control, and the Cave of the Patriarchs is shared under separate prayer arrangements.

entries.name: Gush Katif
entries.text: The bloc of Jewish communities in the southern [[Gaza]] Strip, founded from the 1970s along the coast. Its families built a thriving greenhouse industry that exported vegetables and flowers. In August 2005 Israel evacuated all 21 Jewish communities in Gaza, about 8,000 people, in the [[Disengagement from Gaza]]. Many residents waited years for permanent homes, and the bloc remains a symbol for opponents of territorial withdrawal.

entries.name: Sabra and Shatila massacre
entries.text: From 16 to 18 September 1982, during the [[Lebanon War (1982)]], Lebanese Christian Phalangist militiamen killed hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese civilians in the Sabra and Shatila area of Beirut, which the IDF had surrounded. The killings followed the assassination of the Phalangist leader and president-elect Bashir Gemayel. Israel's Kahan Commission found Israeli leaders indirectly responsible for failing to prevent the massacre, and [[Ariel Sharon]] left the Defense Ministry.

entries.name: Pollard affair
entries.text: Jonathan Pollard, a US Navy intelligence analyst, was arrested in November 1985 for passing classified documents to Israel. He was sentenced to life in prison in 1987. The affair strained relations between Israel and the United States, and Israeli governments campaigned for his release for decades. He was paroled in 2015 and moved to Israel in 2020.

entries.name: Israel-Egypt peace treaty
entries.text: Signed on 26 March 1979 at the White House by [[Menachem Begin]] and Anwar Sadat, with President Jimmy Carter as witness, following the [[Camp David Accords]]. Egypt became the first Arab state to recognize Israel. Israel returned all of [[Sinai]] by April 1982, evacuating its towns there, among them Yamit, and a multinational force still monitors the border. The peace has often been cold, but it has held through wars and revolutions.

entries.name: Taba
entries.text: Beach resort at the head of the Gulf of [[Eilat]], just south of the city. In the 1906 Taba Crisis, Britain, ruling Egypt, forced the [[Ottomans]] to accept a [[Sinai]] border running from Rafah to Taba, the line of today's border. Israel held Taba after 1967 and built a hotel there. When the two countries disagreed on the exact line after the [[Israel-Egypt peace treaty]], international arbitration gave Taba to Egypt, and Israel handed it over in 1989.

entries.name: Narrow waist
entries.text: Between 1949 and 1967 Israel's coastal plain near [[Netanya]] was only about 15 kilometers wide, from the armistice line to the sea. Most of the population and industry lay within range of the hills of [[Judea and Samaria]]. The narrow waist is a central argument in debates over defensible borders and the future of the hill country.

entries.name: Aliyah Bet
entries.text: Clandestine immigration to the Land of Israel from 1934 to 1948, in defiance of British limits, above all the [[White Paper (1939)]]. Most voyages were organized by the [[Haganah]]'s Mossad LeAliyah Bet, many of them after the [[Holocaust]]. More than a hundred ships sailed, and the British intercepted most of them and held tens of thousands of passengers in camps on Cyprus. The ship Exodus 1947 was sent back to Germany, and the outcry helped turn opinion against British rule.

entries.name: Magic Carpet, Operation
entries.text: The 1949 to 1950 airlift that brought about 49,000 Jews from Yemen and Aden to Israel. Many had walked for weeks to reach the camp at Aden. Its Hebrew name, On Eagles' Wings, comes from Exodus 19:4, and many passengers saw the flights as the fulfillment of that promise.

entries.name: Ezra and Nehemiah, Operation
entries.text: The 1951 to 1952 airlift of about 120,000 Jews from [[Iraq]], after Iraq let them leave on condition that they give up their citizenship. Their property was frozen and most arrived with almost nothing. It ended a community that had lived in [[Babylon]] and its successors for some 2,600 years. The operation is named for [[Ezra]] and [[Nehemiah]], who led the [[Return from Babylon]].

entries.name: Moses, Operation
entries.text: The secret airlift of about 8,000 Ethiopian Jews, known as Beta Israel, from refugee camps in Sudan to Israel between November 1984 and January 1985. Thousands had died on the long walk from Ethiopia to Sudan. The flights stopped when news of the operation leaked. It was followed by [[Operation Joshua]] and, in 1991, [[Operation Solomon]].

entries.name: Joshua, Operation
entries.text: A US-led airlift in March 1985, also called Operation Sheba, that flew about 500 Ethiopian Jews left behind in Sudan to Israel after [[Operation Moses]] was cut short. American aircraft landed in the desert near Gedaref to collect them.

entries.name: Solomon, Operation
entries.text: On 24 and 25 May 1991, as rebel forces closed in on Addis Ababa, Israel flew 14,325 Ethiopian Jews to Israel in about 36 hours. Dozens of Israeli aircraft took part, and a single El Al jumbo jet carried more than 1,000 passengers, a world record. It followed [[Operation Moses]] and [[Operation Joshua]].

entries.name: Aliyah from the Soviet Union
entries.text: In the 1970s, after a long struggle by Soviet Jews and their supporters abroad, about 160,000 were allowed to move to Israel. Those refused exit visas, the refuseniks, became a cause around the world. When the Soviet Union opened and collapsed, about a million Jews and their families arrived from 1989 through the 1990s, the largest [[Aliyah]] in the state's history. They transformed Israel's science, technology, medicine, music and politics.

entries.name: Aliyah from North Africa
entries.text: From 1948 through the 1960s most of the Jews of Morocco, Tunisia and Libya moved to Israel, while most Algerian Jews went to France. The secret Operation Yachin of 1961 to 1964 alone brought about 97,000 Jews from Morocco. Many were sent to new development towns in the [[Negev]] and [[Galilee]] and faced hardship and discrimination. Their descendants are now one of the largest parts of Israeli society.

entries.name: Iranian Jews
entries.text: One of the oldest Jewish communities, dating back to the [[Persia]] of [[Cyrus the Great]]. Before the 1979 revolution about 80,000 Jews lived in [[Iran]]. After the execution of the community leader Habib Elghanian that year, most left, chiefly for Israel and the United States. Fewer than 10,000 remain.

entries.name: Aliyah from France
entries.text: French Jews, the largest Jewish community in Europe, began moving to Israel in larger numbers after 2000 as antisemitic attacks rose, among them the Toulouse school shooting of 2012 and the Hyper Cacher attack of 2015. About 7,000 arrived in 2015 alone. Many settled in [[Netanya]], Ashdod and Jerusalem.

entries.name: Aliyah from Ukraine
entries.text: Immigration from Ukraine rose after the war in the east of the country began in 2014 and surged after Russia's invasion in February 2022. That year about 15,000 arrived from Ukraine, along with many more from Russia and Belarus. Israel also took in thousands of Ukrainian refugees who were not eligible under the [[Law of Return]].

entries.name: Aliyah from Latin America
entries.text: Jews from Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil, Mexico and other countries have moved to Israel since 1948, often in waves that followed political or economic crises. Argentina, with the largest community in the region, sent thousands after the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish center in Buenos Aires and especially after the economic collapse of 2001 to 2002.

entries.name: Bnei Menashe
entries.text: A community in the northeast Indian states of Manipur and Mizoram that holds it descends from the tribe of Manasseh, one of the [[Twelve Tribes of Israel]]. In 2005 Israel's Sephardi Chief Rabbi recognized them as descendants of Israel, and several thousand have moved to Israel after formal conversion. India's older Jewish communities, the Bene Israel of Mumbai and the Jews of Cochin, came to Israel mainly in the 1950s and 1960s.

entries.name: Nefesh B'Nefesh
entries.text: Nonprofit founded in 2002 by Rabbi Yehoshua Fass and Tony Gelbart to help Jews from North America and Britain move to Israel. Working with the Israeli government and the [[Jewish Agency for Israel]], it handles paperwork, grants, jobs and community support, and has helped more than 80,000 people make [[Aliyah]].

entries.name: Jewish Agency for Israel
entries.text: Founded in 1929 to represent the Jewish people to the British Mandate authorities and build the national home. Under [[David Ben-Gurion]], who chaired its executive from 1935, it served as the government in waiting of the [[Yishuv]]. Since 1948 it has organized [[Aliyah]] and absorption with the state and links Israel with Jewish communities around the world.

entries.name: Taglit-Birthright Israel
entries.text: Program founded in 1999 by the philanthropists Charles Bronfman and Michael Steinhardt with the Israeli government and Jewish communities abroad. It gives Jewish young adults a free ten-day trip to Israel, and more than 800,000 people from dozens of countries have taken part.

entries.name: Israel National Trail
entries.text: A hiking trail of about 1,100 kilometers that crosses the whole country, from Kibbutz Dan near the Lebanese border to [[Eilat]] on the Red Sea. Opened in 1995 and marked in orange, blue and white, it passes the [[Galilee]], [[Mount Carmel]], the coast, the [[Judean Hills]] and the [[Negev]]. Thru-hikers usually take six to eight weeks.

entries.name: Jesus Trail
entries.text: A walking route of about 65 kilometers opened in 2008 that links places from the life of [[Jesus]] in the [[Galilee]]. It runs from [[Nazareth]] through [[Cana]] and the Horns of Hattin to the [[Sea of Galilee]], the [[Mount of Beatitudes]] and [[Capernaum]].

entries.name: Way of the Patriarchs
entries.text: The ancient road along the ridge of the central hill country, from [[Be'er Sheva]] through [[Hebron]], [[Bethlehem]] and [[Jerusalem]] to [[Shechem]] and north toward the [[Galilee]]. Many of the stories of [[Abraham]], [[Isaac]] and [[Jacob]] take place along it. Route 60 follows much the same line today.

entries.name: Gideon
entries.text: Judge of Israel from the tribe of Manasseh, whose story is told in Judges 6 to 8. With only 300 men carrying trumpets, jars and torches, he routed the Midianite raiders in a night attack from the spring of Harod in the Jezreel Valley. When the people offered him the crown, he refused, saying "The Lord shall rule over you."

entries.name: Mount Sodom
entries.text: A ridge about 11 kilometers long on the southwest shore of the [[Dead Sea]], made largely of rock salt and still below sea level at its top. Rain has carved it into salt caves, among them Malham, one of the longest salt caves in the world. A salt pillar on its cliff is known as Lot's Wife, after the story of [[Sodom and Gomorrah]]. See also [[Lot's Cave]].

entries.name: Dimona
entries.text: Town in the [[Negev]] founded in 1955 and settled mainly by immigrants from North Africa. Nearby is the Shimon Peres Negev Nuclear Research Center, built from the late 1950s with French help under [[Shimon Peres]]. Israel has never confirmed or denied having nuclear weapons, a policy known as ambiguity. Dimona is also home to the African Hebrew Israelites community.

entries.name: Shivta
entries.text: Ruins of a town of the [[Nabataeans]] and [[Byzantines]] in the western [[Negev]], with three churches, streets and houses still standing. With [[Avdat]], Haluza and Mamshit it forms the Incense Route desert cities, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. Its farmers caught rare rainwater to grow crops in the desert.

entries.name: Negev Bedouin
entries.text: About 300,000 Bedouin Arab citizens of Israel who live in the [[Negev]]. Many live in towns such as Rahat, the largest Bedouin city, and Tel Sheva, and many others in villages the state does not recognize. Land claims, planning and poverty are long-running disputes. Some Bedouin volunteer for the [[Israel Defense Forces]], famously as trackers, and Bedouin were among those killed and taken hostage in the [[October 7 attack (2023)]].
